summary: History of the cigarette industry from the 1850s to the 1950s: James Buchanan Duke's machine-made monopoly, mass advertising aimed at children, and the 1950s PR campaign that manufactured doubt about smoking and cancer.

evidence.note: host opens a prehistory of tobacco (Maya, Columbus, Jamestown) treated as background
Crimean War veterans and the first London cigarette factory in 1856 start the story proper
Duke introduced, born 1856 near Durham, enters cigarettes in the 1880s
Bonsack machine deal multiplies output, start of the core story
trading-card inserts lure boys into smoking
monopoly formed, farmers squeezed, unionised hand rollers replaced by machines
anti-smoking crusade aimed at women smokers, morality laws in New York
R. J. Reynolds biography and the launch of Camel
radio and TV sponsorship, Hit Parade, cartoon ads aimed at kids
December 1953 Plaza Hotel meeting where Hill plans the industry response
eugenicist Clarence Cook Little made scientific director of the TIRC
TIRC grant budget by 1963 marks the latest period discussed

notes: Primary subject is an industry/product with no good kind; used practice-or-pseudoscience. Pre-Columbian and early-modern tobacco history (~12 min, part 1) treated as host background, so covered_span starts 1856 and HT/DO/MX are left out of setting. Later industry cover-ups are deferred to future episodes, so reaches_present is false.
